author: Abigail VanderMolen
title: Midland's Pedestrian Plaza boosts visits, but retailers see less benefit - NewsBreak
text:
By Abigail VanderMolen ,
1 hours ago The Downtown Development Authority heard a presentation on Midland's Pedestrian Plaza at its Nov. 12, 2025 meeting at City Hall. (Abigail VanderMolen/Midland Daily News) Pedestrians and restaurants praise Midland’s summertime Pedestrian Plaza, but retailers aren’t feeling the benefits as much, according to survey results shared at Wednesday's Downtown Development Authority meeting.
Since 2020, Midland’s Pedestrian Plaza has closed two blocks of Main Street, from Ashman to Rodd, to motorized traffic throughout the summer, with goals of attracting visitors, showcasing downtown and its businesses, and increasing sales for businesses.
By the numbers
4,900 people attended the June 6 Jedi Mind Trip concert on the Pedestrian Plaza's opening weekend — the most attended Plaza concert of the summer. 34 bands performed in the Pedestrian Plaza over the summer, costing a total of $60,000. 172,000 visits to the Plaza were estimated over the 2025 season. 90%+ of community members repored that they support continuing or expanding the Plaza. $30,000 was spent on marketing the Plaza. $9,229 was spent on Plaza supplies. 57% of businesses report positive impact of the Plaza, and 54% report an increase in sales. “What we can take away from the survey results is that the Pedestrian Plaza really is the number one driver of foot traffic and tourism appeal to downtown Midland in the summertime,” said Selina Harris, Midland community affairs director, who presented the results.
The plaza is popular among community members, with survey results showing over 90% of residents support continuing or expanding the plaza, and data showing the number of visitors continues to increase each year.
From June 6 to September 27, the Plaza received an estimated 172,000 visits lasting an average of 84 minutes each, according to data collected using Placer.ai, which counts the number of cell phones used in an area during a given time. The total count does not represent unique visitors, so it likely includes many repeat visitors.
That amount marks a 3% increase compared to 2024 and a 28% increase compared to 2022.
“What you're seeing is our Pedestrian Plaza has become very well established as people have fallen into the routine of visiting our Pedestrian Plaza, and have brought back friends and neighbors,” Harris said.
The plaza saw its highest volume of visitors between 6 p.m. and 9 p.m., with Fridays and Saturdays being the busiest days
“We have a strong evening and weekend economy built around the music and dining and socializing that goes on downtown, and visitors see Midland as alive, safe and beautiful,” Harris said. “Businesses value the exposure and the brand awareness the Pedestrian Plaza gives them, even when it doesn't necessarily translate into sales that day.”
In total, 57% of businesses reported a positive impact from the survey and 54% said they’d seen higher sales due to the Pedestrian Plaza. Food and beverage sellers had largely positive things to say about its impact, although retail stores tended to see no impact or a negative impact from the plaza.
Harris said retailers on side streets off of Main, especially Ashman, reported that the increase in pedestrians wasn’t translating into an increase in customers.
“They recognize there are a lot more feet on the street in downtown Midland when the Pedestrian Plaza is in place, but (pedestrians) are walking by their store and going to the Pedestrian Plaza and not stopping to shop,” she said.
Harris said survey respondents asked for more accessible parking close to the event venue; a source of shade; and more weekday, Sunday and kid-friendly programming.
The major costs for the Pedestrian Plaza in 2025 were marketing, which cost $30,000; bands, which cost $64,000; and plaza supplies, which cost $9,229, according to an email from Harris, who noted the amount spent on supplies this year was unusually high as the DDA had to replace a set of couch cushions which had been vandalized.
The DDA received $30,000 in money from community sponsors to help cover the cost of the live bands.
Strategic priorities for next year include re-centering the Plaza’s mission of supporting small businesses downtown, finding ways to support retailers downtown, communicating accessible parking opportunities better, and inviting partner organizations to help manage add-on activities.
